covers.title: The Weight of an Empty Car
covers.prompt: Inside the balance room of a grey stone winding house at the foot of a slate hill, late afternoon in wet November, a low oil lamp burning orange against wet stone and a steel cable disappearing up through the ceiling. Close in on one girl, alone in the frame, filling most of it, camera level with her face, three-quarter view from the chest up. She is sixteen, small and wiry, with a round freckled face and dark hair pinned back under a knitted cap. Her jacket is a faded workaday OLIVE, not navy, not black, waxed at the shoulders from the rain, and her sleeves are pushed back above the wrists. She is looking down and slightly away, at something below the frame, with her mouth set and her chin lifted, as if she has just been told the plain truth. One countable anchor object stands alone in the foreground: a single iron balance pan, cut deep and worn shiny at the rim, hanging level on its chain, empty, catching the lamp. Behind her the black grating of a pit and the wet stone of the harbour wall beyond, out of focus.

covers.title: The Boy Who Rode the Grip Down
covers.prompt: A schoolroom in a slate harbour town on a raw grey morning in February, tall windows streaming with rain, three rows of deal desks and a blackboard half wiped. Close in on one boy, alone in the frame, filling most of it, camera level with his face, three-quarter view from the chest up. He is twelve, slight, with straight dark hair combed flat and a smudge of chalk on one cheek, and he is looking directly out of the picture with the particular stillness of somebody working something out. His jersey is a plain BRICK RED, not orange, not maroon, with the cuffs turned back, and over it a white collar his mother has starched too stiff. Held flat against his chest in both hands is one countable anchor object: a single slate pencil, half sharpened, with a leather loop of string tied round its middle. On the desk in front of him, squared up in a row, are four smooth pebbles of increasing size.

covers.title: The Passenger Who Was Not Counted
covers.prompt: The stone terminus at the top of a hill railway, Tannery Moss, on a hard clear morning in late March, the moor behind it going blue and gold and a cold wind moving the smoke from a stove chimney. Close in on one woman, alone in the frame, filling most of it, camera level with her face, three-quarter view from the waist up. She is about forty, tall and plainly dressed for weather, with a lined face and short greying hair blown flat on one side. Her coat is a deep bottle GREEN, not black, not navy, with the collar turned up, and she carries a canvas bag held against her hip with both arms. She is looking straight out past the viewer, past everything, with an expression of perfect stillness. One countable anchor object stands alone in the foreground: the station's open doorway behind her, framing nothing but pale sky and a single bare platform edge.

covers.title: The Ledger of Names at the Winding House
covers.prompt: A low-ceilinged office inside a grey stone winding house, north light from one tall window and a brass lamp on a swing arm, a wet wool coat steaming on a hook behind. Close in on one woman, alone in the frame, filling most of it, three-quarter view from the waist up, leaning over a desk. She is thirty-eight, dark-haired, with spectacles pushed up onto her forehead on a cord and ink on the side of her right hand. Her blouse is a plain GREY, not white, not blue, with the sleeves rolled twice, and over it a knitted vest the colour of strong tea. She is not looking at the viewer; she is looking down at the open book, absorbed, one finger laid flat on the page. One countable anchor object stands alone on the desk in the foreground: a single open calfskin ledger, ruled into three columns, one line of faded ink, and in the margin a fourth ruled space that does not belong. A tin tube lies beside it, capped.

covers.title: A Balance Out of True
covers.prompt: A stone platform part way up a hill railway in a full gale, grey afternoon gone almost black, rain driving sideways across the whole frame and mist flat on the moor behind. Close in on one man, alone in the frame, filling most of it, camera level with his face, three-quarter view from the chest up. He is fifty-two, broad and weathered, with a red face from the wind and grey stubble, and he is looking along the line of the cable and away, jaw clenched, reading the weather. His coat is an oilskin YELLOW, faded to straw, soaked and shining, and his cap has lost its shape entirely. One countable anchor object: a single red woollen mitten on his LEFT hand only, the right hand bare and white to the second joint, gripping a steel brake lever that runs out of the bottom of the frame. The cable runs dead level across the upper third behind him.

covers.title: The Night the Winding House Filled
covers.prompt: The balance room of a grey stone winding house at night, an oil lamp low and the whole space crowded, shadows thrown hard and long up the damp wall. Close in on one young man, alone and clear in the frame, filling most of it, three-quarter view from the waist up, standing very still among the others. He is about twenty-five, hollow-cheeked and unshaven, with fair hair stuck flat to his temple, wearing a clean collar he has not changed out of. His jacket is a good charcoal WOOL, not brown, not green, too fine for the work he does, and his hands hang at his sides, empty and open. He is looking at a point on the stone floor beyond the frame. One countable anchor object stands alone in the foreground: a single iron balance pan on its chain, seen edge-on, with one small lantern hooked to the pit rail burning beside it. Out of focus behind him, the blurred shapes of a dozen other people standing in the dark.

covers.title: The Arithmetic of Consent
covers.prompt: The drum room of a hill railway winding house, a single high window giving hard cold light onto steel, the great cable drum turning behind at half speed. Close in on one man, alone in the frame, filling most of it, camera level with his face, three-quarter view from the waist up. He is sixty-one, spare and upright, with a lined face and a leather apron worn shiny across the front, a horseshoe burn gone brown across the leather. He is looking down at what he is holding, not at the viewer, entirely absorbed. His shirt is a faded workaday BLUE, not white, not grey, with a pencil tucked behind his ear he has plainly forgotten. One countable anchor object stands alone in the foreground: a ruled notebook held open in both hands, filled edge to edge in small neat figures, with a knotted length of steel cable laid diagonally across both pages to hold them flat.

covers.title: The Hands in the Consent Book
covers.prompt: A desk by a tall north window in a stone office, cold grey daylight raking across an open page at a low angle so the ruling stands up off the paper in relief. The composition is dominated by one open calfskin ledger, seen from directly above at a slight angle, filling most of the frame. Two hands enter from the bottom edge and rest on the open page: the left of an old man, knuckles swollen, one finger laid along a ruled line; the right of a younger person, ink on the side, thumb holding a page down. Between them the book's own history is legible in the paper itself — four different ruling patterns, an old line scratched out and rewritten, a new column drawn in a lighter hand, and one narrow margin full of tiny dated entries. A brass desk lamp sits at the top edge, unlit. The cuffs at the wrists are a dark blue wool, worn at the edge.

covers.title: The Counterweight Left Open
covers.prompt: The stone terminus at the top of a hill railway, Tannery Moss, late afternoon in October with the light going long and gold and low across the moor. Close in on one man, alone in the frame, filling most of it, three-quarter view from the chest up, standing in the open doorway of the station. He is fifty-two, broad and weathered, with a red face gone quiet and grey stubble, and he is looking out and down the hill, past everything, with an expression that is neither sad nor glad. His coat is a good oilskin, faded from black to a soft brown at the shoulders, and his cap is pushed back off his head. One countable anchor object: a single red woollen mitten on his LEFT hand only, the right bare and white to the second joint, hanging open at his side. Behind and below him the moor falls away into blue distance, and the cable line runs dead level across the whole of the background.
